claim: FAA guidance recognizes that high-temperature exhaust plumes cause turbulence and vertical shear that can extend over 1,000 feet above the top of a stack or cooling tower, and are most critical in approach and departure corridors.
source_title: AIM 7-6-16 Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes (Smoke Stacks and Cooling Towers)
supporting_excerpt: High temperature exhaust plumes can cause significant air disturbances such as turbulence and vertical shear... significant turbulent effects of an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower... most critical during low altitude flight in calm and cold air, especially in and around approach and departure corridors or airport traffic areas.
caveat: AIM is advisory pilot guidance, not a siting regulation; hosted on third-party mirror (faraim.org) reproducing FAA AIM text.

claim: Aviation regulators treat a critical average vertical plume velocity above 4.3 m/s as a potential hazard to aircraft operations, and require a plume-rise assessment above that threshold.
source_title: CASA Advisory Circular AC 139-05 Plume Rise Assessments
page_or_section: AC 139-05; Civil Aviation Safety Regulations Part 139.370
supporting_excerpt: CASA may determine that plume velocities in excess of 4.3 m/s is or will be a potential hazard to aircraft operations... if the exit vertical velocity is less than 4.3 m/s, no further action is required by the proponent.
caveat: Australian standard; the U.S. FAA has no codified numeric plume-velocity regulation, so 4.3 m/s is an international benchmark, not a U.S. legal threshold.

claim: The FAA developed technical tooling (MITRE Exhaust Plume Analyzer and a Technical Guidance Assessment Tool for Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact) via its Airport Obstruction Standards Committee to evaluate plume impacts near federally obligated airports.
source_title: Technical Guidance Assessment Tool for Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact
supporting_excerpt: FAA's Airport Obstruction Standards Committee (AOSC) was tasked to study the impact exhaust plumes may have on flight safety... MITRE developed the Exhaust-Plume-Analyzer and it is available for no cost.
caveat: Direct PDF fetch returned HTTP 403; content characterized via FAA search-result summary and corroborating aviation-law commentary. Verify exact wording against the FAA PDF before quoting verbatim.

claim: Current FAA wildlife guidance requires separating hazardous-wildlife attractants 10,000 ft from turbine-aircraft airports (5,000 ft for piston), and up to 5 statute miles where the attractant could cause hazardous wildlife movement into approach/departure airspace; new water impoundments of 1/4 acre or larger should not be allowed within an approach corridor or within 5,000 ft of a runway end.
source_title: AC 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or near Airports
supporting_excerpt: 5,000 feet from airports serving piston-powered aircraft, 10,000 feet from airports serving turbine-powered aircraft, and 5 statute miles if the attractant causes hazardous wildlife movement into or across the approach or departure airspace... No new water impoundments of one-quarter acre or larger shall be allowed within an approach corridor and within 5,000 feet from the end of the runway.
caveat: The author's argument cites the cancelled 33B; the current AC is 33C. Exact separation and impoundment wording should be confirmed against the 33C PDF page.

claim: AC 150/5200-33B is cancelled and superseded by AC 150/5200-33C.
source_title: AC 150/5200-33B - Hazardous Wildlife Attractants On or Near Airports (Cancelled)
supporting_excerpt: AC 150/5200-33B - Hazardous Wildlife Attractants On or Near Airports (Cancelled)

claim: FAA's 2012 interim RPZ land-use guidance requires ADO/Regional consultation with the National Airport Planning and Environmental Division whenever buildings, structures, above-ground utilities, parking, or hazmat/fuel storage would be located within a Runway Protection Zone, and requires documenting alternatives to avoid or mitigate the encroachment.
source_title: FAA Interim Guidance on Land Uses Within a Runway Protection Zone (ACRP Web Resource)
page_or_section: Summary of FAA 2012 RPZ interim guidance memorandum
supporting_excerpt: consult with the National Airport Planning and Environmental Division whenever an airport project, local development project, or change in RPZ dimensions would result in buildings and structures or specific land uses being located within the RPZ, including... parking lots, fuel storage facilities, hazardous materials storage, and aboveground utilities.
caveat: Secondary source summarizing the FAA memorandum; cite the underlying 2012 FAA RPZ memo for a primary reference.

claim: FAA obstruction evaluation criteria hold that a structure has a substantial adverse effect if it causes electromagnetic interference to an air navigation or radar/surveillance facility or the signal used by aircraft.
source_title: FAA Procedures for Handling Airspace Matters (PHAM), Ch. 6 Sec. 3 - Identifying/Evaluating Aeronautical Effect
supporting_excerpt: a proposed structure would have a substantial adverse effect if it causes electromagnetic interference to the operation of an air navigation or radar/surveillance facility or the signal used by aircraft.
caveat: Characterized from FAA search-result excerpt; verify exact clause in the live PHAM section.

claim: IAD set a 19-year passenger record in 2024 with 27.25 million passengers (10.38 million international), even as aircraft movements declined by roughly 2,000 versus 2023, with growth driven by international widebody traffic.
source_title: This Washington DC Airport Set Not 1, But 2 New Records In 2024
supporting_excerpt: broke a 19-year passenger record with 27.25 million passengers... 10.38 million were international... the number of aircraft movements at the airport declined by over 2,000 in 2024 compared to 2023.
caveat: Trade-press reporting; confirm against MWAA/ACI official traffic statistics for citation-grade use.

claim: MWAA's 2025 Dulles master plan envisions growth to 90 million annual passengers and protects for a future fifth runway (12R/30L), indicating long-horizon runway-capacity demand.
source_title: New master plan for Dulles Airport envisions growth to 90 million annual passengers
supporting_excerpt: The plan envisions an ultimate capacity of 90 million passengers annually... calls for a fifth runway... designated Runway 12R/30L.
caveat: Press summary of master plan; corroborated by MWAA/flydulles D2 fifth-runway page. Use MWAA master plan document for primary citation.

claim: IAD Runway 1L/19R (the runway whose approach/departure surface contains the proposed parcel) is the newest north-south runway, completed in 2008 at approximately 9,400 ft long and 150 ft wide.
supporting_excerpt: The fourth runway is a north-south runway, approximately 9,400 feet long and 150 feet wide... completed in 2008 and was designated Runway 1L/19R.

claim: Data centers commonly rely on diesel backup generators that run 50-150 test-hours per year each; a single 2.5 MW unit emits roughly 1.2 metric tons of NOx and 0.05 t of particulates annually during testing, making a data-center campus a concentrated exhaust/thermal source.
source_title: Data Centers' Use of Diesel Generators for Backup Power Is Commonplace and Problematic
supporting_excerpt: tested monthly, resulting in 50 to 150 hours of annual operation per generator... a single 2.5 MW diesel generator... emitting approximately 1.2 metric tons of NOx and 0.05 metric tons of PM per year during testing.
units: hours/year; metric tons NOx and PM per generator
caveat: General industry figures, not IAD-specific; illustrates the plume/exhaust source character, not the specific proposal's emissions.
